payload.passage:
There is a peculiar vanity in the modern conservator's creed that a building should be returned to the condition in which its architect intended it to be seen. The creed presupposes, first, that the architect's intentions can be recovered, and second, that they were singular, coherent and uncompromised by the exigencies of budget, weather and patrons' whims. Neither presupposition survives even a cursory acquaintance with the archives. Most cathedrals, for instance, were never finished in any sense that their builders would have recognised; they were abandoned, resumed, amended and quietly improved across centuries by men who held no reverence whatever for the work of their predecessors. To freeze such a structure at a single moment and call the result 'original' is less an act of fidelity than of selection, and selection, however scrupulously documented, is a form of authorship.

None of this is to suggest that conservation is a fraud. The more defensible position, advanced by a minority of practitioners who are rarely invited to the ribbon-cuttings, holds that a building is best understood as a record of its own repairs. A Georgian window set into a medieval wall, a Victorian buttress propping up a Norman nave: these are not blemishes upon an otherwise legible text but the very grammar in which that text was written. The conservator who scrapes them away in pursuit of purity resembles an editor who, having discovered that a poem was revised, restores the first draft and burns the rest.

Why, then, does the purist impulse persist? Partly, one suspects, because it flatters the present. To declare that we have recovered the original is to claim a transparent relationship with the past, unmediated by our own preoccupations, and it spares us the discomfort of admitting that every restoration reveals at least as much about its own age as about the age it purports to revive. The grey, antiseptic interiors favoured by mid-twentieth-century restorers now look unmistakably of their decade, as dated in their way as the gilded excesses they replaced. Our own preferred idiom, with its fastidious visible joints and honestly labelled materials, will no doubt appear equally quaint to successors who will, in their turn, be certain they have finally got it right.
payload.question: Which statement best captures the writer's central contention about restoration?
options: Conservators ought to abandon restoration and let buildings decay naturally.

Architects' intentions are well documented but are ignored by modern conservators.
Mid-twentieth-century restorers were more faithful to original buildings than their successors.
payload.explanation_uz: Muallif asl holatga qaytarish tanlash va muallifliq ekanini aytadi ("selection ... is a form of authorship") va keyingi qo'shimchalarni 'grammatika' deb ataydi.

payload.passage:
The decline of the amateur naturalist is usually narrated as a story of progress, and the narrators are seldom disinterested. In the nineteenth century, the clergyman with a microscope or the widow with a herbarium might contribute observations of genuine value to the learned societies, and was received, if not always as an equal, then at least as a colleague. By the early twentieth century the doors had narrowed. Specialisation produced journals whose prose was calculated to repel the uninitiated, and credentials replaced curiosity as the currency of admission. That this made science more rigorous is the received view; that it also made it more parochial is a suspicion voiced less often.

It would be tendentious to claim that nothing was gained. The enthusiast's notebooks, charming as they are, were frequently unsystematic, and a great many confident identifications turned out to be the product of wishful seeing. Yet the professional's habit of treating the unusual as noise to be filtered is not obviously superior to the amateur's habit of treating it as an invitation. Several of the more consequential anomalies in the history of the field were first recorded by people with no standing to record them, and were ignored for decades precisely because of who they were.

Recent years have witnessed a partial and somewhat self-congratulatory rehabilitation. Projects that enlist thousands of volunteers to photograph, count and log are hailed as a democratisation of knowledge, though the volunteers are generally issued with protocols so rigid that their role is closer to that of instruments than of investigators. They are invited to collect, not to wonder; the questions remain the property of those with letters after their names. One may applaud the data while doubting that the old amateur's freedom has been restored. What has been revived is his labour, not his licence.

Whether the distinction matters depends on what one believes science is for. If its purpose is merely to accumulate reliable facts, the volunteer with a checklist will do admirably. If it is also a cultural practice, a way of cultivating attention and tolerating perplexity, then something has been lost that no dataset, however large, will register.
payload.question: Which statement best summarises the writer's argument?
options: Professional scientists have wrongly excluded all volunteers from research.
Nineteenth-century amateurs were generally more accurate than professionals.
Volunteer data projects are worthless because their data are unreliable.
Modern volunteer projects restore the amateur's labour but not the intellectual independence that once defined amateurs.
payload.explanation_uz: Oxirgi xulosa: "What has been revived is his labour, not his licence" - mehnat qaytdi, erkinlik emas.

payload.passage:
The station at Verlenne has been closed for so long that the town has begun to treat its absence as a civic achievement. Where trains once discharged commercial travellers and the occasional bride, there is now a car park of exemplary tidiness, from which the municipality derives a modest income and the visitor a sense of having arrived nowhere in particular. I went back in October, ostensibly to settle the affairs of an aunt, in truth to test a theory of my own: that places we have loved are never so much altered as revealed, their shabbiness having been present all along, concealed by the generosity of our attention.

The theory, I regret to report, was not vindicated. The café opposite, which in memory dispensed coffee of almost liturgical darkness, had become a purveyor of artisanal sourdough, and the proprietor, a young man whose beard had clearly been the subject of more deliberation than his menu, assured me that nobody in living memory had ever served anything else there. I did not contradict him. It is a curious feature of returning that one is cast at once as the unreliable witness, the elderly sentimentalist whose recollections are to be received with the polite indulgence reserved for relatives at weddings.

And yet I could not quite dismiss my own evidence. The clock above the vanished ticket hall, preserved by some committee's whim and stopped at ten past four, struck me as the only honest object in the vicinity, since it alone declined to pretend that time had continued. Everything else had been briskly renewed, and renewal, I reflected, is merely forgetting conducted with a budget. The town was not worse for it; by any reasonable measure it was cleaner, safer and better fed. But I stood for some while before that arrested face with the vague conviction that I had been robbed of something I could not itemise, and that the thief, if he could be found, would turn out to be entirely innocent, being nothing more sinister than the passage of thirty years and a talent for improvement.
payload.question: The narrator's tone in describing the visit is best characterised as
options: bitterly accusatory towards the townspeople
enthusiastically approving of the changes
wistful yet wryly self-deprecating
coldly analytical and detached
payload.explanation_uz: Muallif o'zini "elderly sentimentalist" deb kuladi, ammo yo'qotishdan afsuslanadi - xo'rsinish va o'ziga kinoya.

payload.passage:
Efficiency is among the few virtues that modern institutions pursue without feeling obliged to define it. To be efficient is to eliminate waste, and waste is whatever the person wielding the spreadsheet cannot immediately justify. What this habit of mind overlooks is that many arrangements which appear wasteful in ordinary times are, in extraordinary ones, the sole difference between resilience and collapse. A hospital that runs at ninety-eight per cent occupancy is a triumph of management until the day it is asked to absorb a sudden influx of patients, whereupon its triumph is revealed as a debt that was merely deferred.

Slack, as economists of a certain temperament call it, is therefore best understood not as the opposite of efficiency but as its insurance premium. The difficulty is that premiums are visible and payouts are not: no one thanks the administrator for the catastrophe that failed to occur because a spare ward remained unstaffed. Prudence, unlike profligacy, leaves no monument. Consequently the incentives within any organisation tilt steadily towards the trimming of reserves, and those who resist are cast as sentimentalists, obstructing reforms that on paper have proved their worth every quarter.

It would be naive to infer that all redundancy is wise. Bureaucracies are perfectly capable of manufacturing surplus out of sheer inertia, and the committee that exists because it has always existed is hardly a bulwark against anything. The real task, which is considerably harder than either slashing or hoarding, lies in distinguishing slack that protects from slack that merely accumulates. No formula will accomplish this; it demands judgement about contingencies that, by definition, have not yet happened and cannot be costed with precision.

That such judgement is unfashionable is hardly surprising. We have grown accustomed to treating the measurable as the real and the unmeasured as indulgence. But a system optimised exclusively for the conditions it expects is, in a quite literal sense, unprepared, and it is a peculiar form of rationality that congratulates itself for being right about a future which then declines to arrive on schedule.
payload.question: The central argument of the passage is that
options: institutions should retain spare capacity but must distinguish protective surplus from merely inert surplus
efficiency is an illusory goal that should be abandoned
hospitals are poorly managed because of an obsession with occupancy
bureaucracies should hold large reserves of every kind to be safe
payload.explanation_uz: Muallif 'slack'ni sug'urta deb biladi, lekin "distinguishing slack that protects from slack that merely accumulates" muhimligini aytadi.

Efficiency is among the few virtues that modern institutions pursue without feeling obliged to define it. To be efficient is to eliminate waste, and waste is whatever the person wielding the spreadsheet cannot immediately justify. What this habit of mind overlooks is that many arrangements which appear wasteful in ordinary times are, in extraordinary ones, the sole difference between resilience and collapse. A hospital that runs at ninety-eight per cent occupancy is a triumph of management until the day it is asked to absorb a sudden influx of patients, whereupon its triumph is revealed as a debt that was merely deferred.

Slack, as economists of a certain temperament call it, is therefore best understood not as the opposite of efficiency but as its insurance premium. The difficulty is that premiums are visible and payouts are not: no one thanks the administrator for the catastrophe that failed to occur because a spare ward remained unstaffed. Prudence, unlike profligacy, leaves no monument. Consequently the incentives within any organisation tilt steadily towards the trimming of reserves, and those who resist are cast as sentimentalists, obstructing reforms that on paper have proved their worth every quarter.

It would be naive to infer that all redundancy is wise. Bureaucracies are perfectly capable of manufacturing surplus out of sheer inertia, and the committee that exists because it has always existed is hardly a bulwark against anything. The real task, which is considerably harder than either slashing or hoarding, lies in distinguishing slack that protects from slack that merely accumulates. No formula will accomplish this; it demands judgement about contingencies that, by definition, have not yet happened and cannot be costed with precision.

That such judgement is unfashionable is hardly surprising. We have grown accustomed to treating the measurable as the real and the unmeasured as indulgence. But a system optimised exclusively for the conditions it expects is, in a quite literal sense, unprepared, and it is a peculiar form of rationality that congratulates itself for being right about a future which then declines to arrive on schedule.

options: obstacle to progress
protective defence

subject of debate
payload.explanation_uz: 'Bulwark' - himoya vositasi; qo'mita hech narsadan himoya qilmaydi, degan ma'no.

payload.passage:
Every few years a list circulates of words said to be untranslatable: a Portuguese term for a particular species of longing, a Japanese phrase for the light filtering through leaves, a Welsh coinage for the comfort of home. The lists are shared with the rapture usually reserved for discoveries, and they rest on a confusion so elementary that it is remarkable how seldom it is pointed out. A word is untranslatable, in these accounts, if it cannot be rendered by a single word in another language. By that standard almost every word is untranslatable, and the claim reduces to the observation, not strikingly profound, that languages divide up the world with different scissors.

What the lists really testify to is the enthusiasm of the monoglot for the exotic. The Welsh speaker who encounters the coinage in a greeting card is unlikely to experience it as a metaphysical marvel; she simply uses it. Her English neighbour, meanwhile, is not thereby barred from understanding the sentiment, only from conveying it economically. Explanation takes longer than a word, but length is a matter of convenience and not of comprehension. Were it otherwise, no one would ever have been moved by a translated novel, and the history of world literature would consist of a series of polite misunderstandings.

Nor should the sceptic's case be pressed too far. Translation does lose things, and anyone who has watched a joke die in transit knows that connotation, rhythm and allusion are less obliging than denotation. The point is that such losses are graded, local and negotiable, whereas the rhetoric of untranslatability suggests something absolute, a wall instead of a toll. A translator does not stand before a wall; she stands before a toll booth, and must decide, case by case, what is worth paying. The best translations are not those that forfeit nothing, which is an impossible standard, but those whose losses are chosen with intelligence and whose compensations are made with a certain nerve.

It is rather a pity that the more interesting question is so rarely asked: not whether a word can cross, but what it costs, and who decides.
payload.question: The writer's main point is that
options: translation between languages with different cultures is impossible
claims of untranslatability exaggerate what are in fact graded, negotiable losses
a single-word equivalent can always be found with enough effort
lists of untranslatable words are valuable guides for translators
payload.explanation_uz: Muallif 'devor emas, to'lov joyi' deydi: yo'qotishlar darajali va kelishiladigan, mutlaq emas.
